sections.html:
Boulder sits where the plains meet the Rocky Mountain foothills, roughly 25 miles northwest of Denver. It is a home rule city and the county seat. Population was 108,250 in the 2020 census, with a 2024 estimate of 106,803.

With a university, research labs and a few large companies as anchors, some owners arrive or leave on a job's timetable and need a sale that fits it. Weather is the other local factor. An average season brings 88 inches of snow, and summers bring frequent afternoon thunderstorms. On foothill lots, inspectors check the roof and the drainage first, and a tired roof usually shows up in the price talk.

Boulder calls itself the number one flash flood risk community in Colorado, and anyone buying a house in a mapped floodplain will have to sort out insurance.

  • Flood coverage on most policies does not start for 30 days, so a buyer who shops late may close without it.
  • Since the city joined the Community Rating System in 1992 and reached a Class 5 rating in early 2013, standard policyholders get a 25% discount.
  • A surveyor with a Colorado license can prepare an elevation certificate, which can bring premiums down. The city lets you search for certificates already filed.
  • New residential construction must sit at least two feet above the 100-year flood elevation.

Pull up the city's interactive floodplain map and find your lot before you list or accept an offer. If a certificate exists, give the title company a copy so the buyer's insurer gets it fast.

sections.h2: Why the 2013 flood still comes up
sections.html:
Rain began around September 9, 2013, and the flooding was worst on September 11 and 12. Several spots in the city recorded 15 to 20 inches between September 9 and 15. Boulder County averages about 20.7 inches in a whole year, meaning five days delivered a full year of rain.

On September 12 Boulder Creek ran above 5,000 cubic feet per second. Its normal flow is 150 to 200. In the county, 262 homes were destroyed and nearly 300 more were damaged, and three deaths were confirmed. A major disaster was declared for the county.

Buyers and lenders know this history, so floodplain questions arrive early in a Boulder sale. Collect your flood zone status, elevation certificate and past insurance claims before the first showing, or before you talk to a cash buyer.

sections.h2: What the Marshall Fire means for county sellers
sections.html:
The Marshall Fire burned in Boulder County from December 30, 2021, to January 1, 2022. Superior was evacuated first and Louisville was ordered out later. Around 1,084 structures burned, another 149 were damaged, and the fire covered 6,026 acres in winds gusting to 115 mph.

The sheriff's office announced in June 2023 that the cause involved two separate occurrences: embers on the Twelve Tribes property and a sparking Xcel Energy power line. Superior and Louisville, not the city of Boulder, took the damage. Even so, a buyer of any county house may ask about fire history and insurance.

Before anyone can use or advertise a Boulder house as a rental, the city must approve a rental license. The approval rests on inspections of health and safety, mechanical systems and energy efficiency, and expect it to take several weeks at minimum.

The efficiency piece is SmartRegs, which requires all rental housing in the city to meet a basic energy standard. Owners can reach compliance through a prescriptive pathway or a performance pathway, and the city lists the inspection companies that can do the work. Contractors should write invoices that describe the work done, because the SmartRegs inspector uses them to update the property score. Tenants can even earn the landlord a point by taking the SmartRegs tenant quiz.

Selling a former rental? Say whether the license is current. Whoever buys it to rent it out must start this process, and the SmartRegs guide is written with realtors in that spot in mind.

sections.h2: How Boulder property taxes are paid
sections.html:
Boulder County bills the tax. Residential assessment rates for 2026 are 6.8% for local governments and 7.05% for schools, and they apply to the whole county.

Payment optionDue date
Full paymentApril 30
First halfLast day of February
Second halfJune 15

Once the sale records, tax statements go to the mailing address written on the deed, so the buyer should double-check it. The title company splits the current year's bill between you and the buyer at the closing table. Behind on taxes? Request a payoff figure first, then pick the closing date.

sections.h2: Recording the deed in Boulder County
sections.html:
Deeds are filed with the Boulder County Clerk and Recorder. Recording a document costs $43 as of July 1, 2025. On a transfer deed over $500, the state also assesses a documentary fee of $.01 per $100, and the purchase contract usually says who pays.

The counter is open Monday through Thursday, 7:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., with drop boxes in Boulder, Lafayette and Longmont. Paperwork needs at least a one-inch top margin or the recorder can turn it away, which is one more reason to let the title company prepare it.

sections.h2: What to gather before you sell
sections.html:
A short folder saves days at the title company, whichever way you sell.

  • Your tax statement, or a payoff figure if anything is past due.
  • The flood zone result for your address and any elevation certificate on file.
  • For a former rental, the license and the SmartRegs paperwork, including contractor invoices that describe the work done.
  • Any insurance claim history for roof, water or fire damage.
  • Names and contact details for everyone on the title.

None of this has to be perfect. If something is missing, say so up front and the title company can usually track it down while the sale moves along.

sections.h2: What are your options for selling a Boulder house?
sections.html:
The usual routes are a listing, a sale by owner, or a cash offer. Flood exposure, an unlicensed rental past or deferred maintenance can slow a listing, since each prompts more questions from buyers, lenders and insurers.

A cash sale is as is. Nobody orders repairs and nobody waits on a loan. The steps:

  1. Send us the Boulder address and tell us about the house: flood zone, any rental use, and how the roof looks.
  2. We go over the details and write an offer for the house in its current state.
  3. If you accept, a title company opens the file, looks for tax debt and liens, and drafts the deed.
  4. You sign, the county records the deed, and the money goes to you at closing.

Declining the offer costs you nothing. Send the address and we will walk through how a sale of your house would go.

faqs.q: What happened in Boulder during the 2013 flood?
faqs.a: On September 12, 2013 the creek peaked above 5,000 cubic feet per second, and 262 county homes were destroyed. Floodplain questions still arrive early in a sale.

faqs.q: Is my Boulder house in a flood zone?
faqs.a: Parts of the city are. The interactive floodplain map shows your lot. Because coverage takes 30 days to start, a buyer should apply early.

faqs.q: Do I need a rental license to rent my Boulder house?
faqs.a: Yes. The city has to approve a rental license first, and that review includes the SmartRegs energy standard.

faqs.q: What does it cost to record a deed in Boulder County?
faqs.a: Recording runs $43 per document as of July 1, 2025. A transfer deed over $500 also owes the state's $.01 per $100 documentary fee.

faqs.q: When are Boulder property taxes due?
faqs.a: Pay it all by April 30, or split it: the first half falls on the last day of February and the second on June 15.
